implementation_notes: The stdlib primitive is Timeout.timeout(sec): it runs the block while a watchdog thread waits for it to finish and raises Timeout::Error (or the supplied class) when the budget expires, and when a Fiber scheduler is defined the timeout is delegated to Scheduler#timeout_after so async I/O libraries implement it themselves. For network calls the better realization is the client's own budget - Net::HTTP's open_timeout, read_timeout and write_timeout, or the equivalent option of the HTTP client in use - because that aborts the syscall instead of raising asynchronously inside whatever the block was doing. Timeout.timeout is therefore a library fallback rather than a language guarantee, and its own documentation warns that it cannot be relied on for blocks that use ensure or rescue broadly.
code_sketch:
require 'timeout'
begin
  status = Timeout.timeout(2) { client.call }     # raises Timeout::Error
rescue Timeout::Error
  raise ServiceUnavailable, 'dependency timed out'
end
# preferred for HTTP: http.open_timeout = 1; http.read_timeout = 2
pitfalls: The exception is delivered asynchronously from the watchdog thread and can be prevented by an ensure or a broad rescue inside the block; the documentation states that the method cannot be relied on to enforce timeouts for untrusted blocks.
A value of 0 or nil executes the block without any timeout, so a configuration default of zero silently means 'wait forever'.
Blocking C extensions that never yield to the scheduler cannot be interrupted, and with a Fiber scheduler the timeout is only as effective as the scheduler's hooks.
All Timeout.timeout calls share one watchdog thread and a global request queue, so a large number of concurrent timeouts serializes their bookkeeping through it.
